title: Shopping, clothes and colors
objectives: I can ask for clothes in a size and a color, and ask what they cost.
I can point things out with 'цей' and 'той' in the nominative and the accusative, and tell 'це' the pointer from 'це' the neuter of 'цей'.
I can make color adjectives agree with their nouns, including the plural-only nouns 'штани́' and 'гро́ші'.
I can say whether something is cheap or expensive, and use 'ко́штує' or 'ко́штують' to match the thing that costs.
I can ask permission with 'мо́жна' and an infinitive, and explain how 'соро́чка', 'жо́втий' and 'гро́ші' are pronounced.

vocabulary.note: Its other forms are 'ця' (feminine), 'це' (neuter) and 'ці' (plural). It points at something near the speaker. The 'ц' is hard before 'е' and soft in 'ця', 'цю' and 'ці'.
Its other forms are 'та' (feminine), 'те' (neuter) and 'ті' (plural). It points at something farther from the speaker.
A shirt with a collar and buttons, worn by men and women. The 'ч' is hard, as Ukrainian 'ч' always is before a consonant. The accusative is 'соро́чку'.
The 'н' is soft before 'я', while the 'к' before it stays hard. The accusative is 'су́кню' and the nominative plural 'су́кні'.
It has no singular: one pair of pants is 'штани́', and every word that agrees with it is plural ('ці штани́', 'мої́ штани́').
A short coat for outdoors. The accusative is 'ку́ртку'.

It is cited in the plural, the form for a pair. One shoe is 'череви́к', genitive 'череви́ка', so this is an ordinary plural, unlike 'штани́'. It names closed shoes that cover the foot, up to the ankle.
A hard stem: 'черво́на', 'черво́не', 'черво́ні'. The 'в' before a vowel is [ʋ].
The 'в' comes before a consonant, so it is said [w], as in 'cow': [ˈʒɔwtɪj].

example.source: The yellow bus is standing at the stop.

vocabulary.note: The first, unstressed 'е' leans toward 'и'; the stressed 'е' is a clear [ɛ].

example.source: The park is big and green.

vocabulary.note: 'Чо́рна ка́ва' is coffee without milk, as 'black coffee' is in English.
A hard stem: 'бі́ла', 'бі́ле', 'бі́лі'. The 'б' is only slightly softened before 'і'.
The 'с' is soft before 'і'. A hard stem: 'сі́ра', 'сі́ре', 'сі́рі'.
The stress stays on the ending in every form: 'дорога́', 'дороге́', 'дорогі́'. It also means 'dear' about a person, for example at the start of a letter.
The 'ш' is hard before 'е'. The forms are 'деше́ва', 'деше́ве', 'деше́ві'.

example.source: Cheese is cheap at the market.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'ро́зміру'. A size is said as a number after the noun: 'ро́змір со́рок ві́сім', size forty-eight.
The 'ц' is soft before 'і'.
It has no singular, so it takes plural words where English uses singular ones: 'мої́ гро́ші', my money; 'Гро́ші тут.', the money is here.
'купу́ю', 'купу́єш', 'купу́ють': in the present '-ува-' becomes '-у-', as in 'працюва́ти'.

example.source: I am buying bread and milk.

vocabulary.note: Regular, like 'чита́ти': 'приміря́ю', 'приміря́єш'. The 'р' is soft before 'я'.

example.source: Oksana is trying on a dress.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: соро́чка, жо́втий, гро́ші and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
Every new word in this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. Nothing here needs a new rule. The points below are the ones that are easy to miss, in the order of the reading procedure: the letters first, then softness, then the stress.

Ukrainian 'ч' is a hard consonant. The tongue stays flat and the sound is [t͡ʃ], as in 'church', before every vowel and before a consonant: 'соро́чка' [sɔˈrɔt͡ʃkɑ], 'чо́рний', 'череви́ки'. Like the other consonants that cannot be fully soft, it is only slightly softened before 'і'. The soft sign never follows 'ч', so no spelling ever asks for a soft 'ч'.

The letter 'в' has two sounds. Before a vowel it is [ʋ], between English 'v' and 'w' ('черво́ний', 'деше́вий', 'череви́ки'). At the end of a syllable, before a consonant, it is [w], as in 'cow': 'жо́втий' is [ˈʒɔwtɪj], and its 'ов' sounds close to the 'ow' of English 'bowl'. The 'в' never turns into [f].

In 'гро́ші' [ˈɦrɔʃi] the 'г' is the voiced [ɦ] of the second alphabet unit, and the 'ш' stays the [ʃ] of 'shoe', only slightly softened by the 'і' after it. The 'ш' of 'деше́вий' is fully hard before 'е'.

Softness works as the unit on soft sounds taught:

- 'ц' is hard before 'е' ('цей') and soft before 'і', 'я' and 'ю' ('ціна́', 'ця', 'цю'); in 'цьо́го' the soft sign plus 'о' writes the same soft 'ц' before [ɔ].
- In 'су́кня' [ˈsuknʲɑ] only the 'н' is soft; the 'к' before it stays hard.
- In 'приміря́ти' the 'р' is soft because 'я' follows it, and the 'м' is slightly softened before 'і'.
- 'с' is soft before 'і' in 'сі́рий'; 'б' is only slightly softened in 'бі́лий'.

Unstressed 'е' leans toward 'и', as the unit on stress explained: the first two vowels of 'череви́ки' and the first 'е' of 'зеле́ний' sound a little like 'и', while the stressed 'е' of 'зеле́ний' and 'деше́вий' is a clear [ɛ].

Two verbs show how the present can move the stress. 'Купува́ти' belongs to the family of 'працюва́ти': in the present '-ува-' becomes '-у-', and the stress falls on that 'у': 'купу́ю', 'купу́єш', 'купу́ють'. 'Коштува́ти' makes the same change but puts the stress on its first syllable: 'ко́штує', 'ко́штують'. This is why the stress of a present tense is learned from the 'я' and 'ти' forms.

Two nouns show that an 'і' in a closed syllable may or may not alternate. 'Ро́змір' keeps its 'і' in every form ('ро́зміру'), unlike 'стіл', 'стола́', so the genitive is learned with the noun. 'Ко́лір', color, does alternate: its other forms use the stem 'ко́льор-' ('ко́льору'), where the 'л' that was soft before 'і' stays soft and is written 'ль' before 'о'.

rows: before і, я, ю or ьо

examples.source: I am trying on a jacket.

grammar.title: Цей and той: this and that
grammar.explanation:
A demonstrative pronoun is a word that points out a particular person or thing, as 'this' and 'that' do in 'this shirt' and 'that jacket'. Ukrainian has two, and each agrees with its noun in gender, number and case, exactly as an adjective does:

- 'цей' points at something near the speaker: 'цей ро́змір', 'ця соро́чка', 'це вікно́', 'ці штани́'.
- 'той' points at something farther away: 'той магази́н', 'та су́кня', 'те мі́сто', 'ті череви́ки'.

In the accusative, the case of the object, they change exactly where an adjective changes (the unit on food and drink):

- The feminine takes '-ю' or '-у': 'Я хо́чу цю ку́ртку.', 'Я купу́ю ту су́кню.'
- The neuter and the plural of things stay as they are: 'Я ба́чу це вікно́.', 'Я купу́ю ці штани́.'
- The masculine of a thing stays as it is: 'Я купу́ю цей стіл.'
- The masculine of a person or an animal takes '-ого', like 'ново́го дру́га': 'цьо́го', 'того́' ('Ви ба́чите того́ чолові́ка?').

People in the plural have another accusative form, which comes with the plural cases in A2; this unit uses the plural only for things.

A demonstrative can stand without its noun when the noun is clear from the situation. 'Я хо́чу цю.' means 'I want this one': English adds 'one', while the Ukrainian ending already shows which noun is meant (here a feminine one, such as 'ку́ртка'). A shop assistant may ask 'Ця чи та?', 'This one or that one?'

Two words are spelled 'це', and they do different jobs:

- 'Це' the pointer, from the unit on people and things, never changes and introduces whatever it points at, of any gender or number. The sentence has no word for 'is', and English adds one: 'Це су́кня.' 'This is a dress.'; 'Це мої́ штани́.' 'These are my pants.'
- 'це' the neuter of 'цей' agrees with a neuter noun and stands directly before it: 'це вікно́', 'this window'.

Word order tells them apart. In 'Ця су́кня черво́на.', 'This dress is red', the word 'ця' agrees with 'су́кня', and the color after the noun is the predicate. In 'Це черво́на су́кня.', 'This is a red dress', the word 'це' points, and 'черво́на су́кня' is what it points at. With a neuter noun the two words look the same, so only the order decides: 'Це вікно́ вели́ке.' is 'This window is big', and 'Це вели́ке вікно́.' is 'This is a big window'.

rows: цей, той; цьо́го, того́ for a person or animal

examples.target: Ця ку́ртка си́ня, а та сі́ра.
examples.source: This jacket is blue, and that one is gray.
examples.source_literal: This jacket blue, and that gray.

grammar.title: Colors, plural-only nouns and prices
grammar.explanation:
Color words in Ukrainian are adjectives, so they agree with their noun in gender, number and case. Most of them have a hard stem and the endings of 'нови́й': '-ий' masculine, '-а' feminine, '-е' neuter and '-і' plural. The hard-stem colors of this unit are:

- 'черво́ний', red
- 'жо́втий', yellow
- 'зеле́ний', green
- 'чо́рний', black
- 'бі́лий', white
- 'сі́рий', gray

'Си́ній', blue, has a soft stem, so its endings are '-ій', '-я', '-є' and '-і': 'си́ня су́кня', 'си́нє вікно́', 'си́ні штани́'. The word for color itself is 'ко́лір', a masculine noun: 'Яки́й ко́лір?', 'What color?'

A color can stand before its noun as a description or after it as the predicate, with no word for 'is': 'бі́ла соро́чка', 'a white shirt'; 'Соро́чка бі́ла.', 'The shirt is white.'

The object of 'хоті́ти', 'купува́ти' or 'приміря́ти' is in the accusative, and the color changes with it: the feminine ending '-а' becomes '-у' and '-я' becomes '-ю' ('Я хо́чу зеле́ну соро́чку.', 'Я купу́ю си́ню су́кню.'), while masculine and neuter things and the plural of things keep the nominative form ('Ти хо́чеш бі́лий хліб?').

A plural-only noun is a noun that has only plural forms, even when it names one thing. 'Штани́' is one pair of pants, and 'гро́ші' is money. Every word that agrees with such a noun is plural, and so is the verb:

- 'Ці штани́ сі́рі.' 'These pants are gray.'
- 'Мої́ гро́ші тут.' 'My money is here.'

English treats 'pants' the same way ('these pants are'), but it treats 'money' as singular ('my money is'), so 'гро́ші' needs care: where English says 'my money is', Ukrainian uses plural forms. 'Череви́ки' is different again. It is the ordinary plural of 'череви́к', one shoe, which has a singular of its own: 'Цей череви́к мали́й.', 'This shoe is small.'

Prices follow the same agreement. In 'Скі́льки ко́штує ця су́кня?' the thing is the subject, so 'коштува́ти' agrees with it: 'ко́штує' for one thing, 'ко́штують' for a plural or a plural-only noun ('Скі́льки ко́штують ці штани́?'). The question word comes first, and Ukrainian needs no helper verb where English puts 'does' before the subject ('How much does this dress cost?'). A noun subject usually follows the verb ('Скі́льки ко́штує ця су́кня?'), and a pronoun subject usually comes before it ('Скі́льки вона́ ко́штує?'). The answer gives the number with the forms of 'гри́вня' from the unit on numbers: 'Вона́ ко́штує сто гри́вень.', 'Вони́ ко́штують дев’яно́сто гри́вень.'

examples.source: How much does this dress cost?

grammar.title: Мо́жна with an infinitive: asking permission
grammar.explanation:
The unit on food and drink introduced 'мо́жна' as a predicative word: a word that is the whole predicate of a sentence with no grammatical subject. 'Мо́жна ка́ву?' is literally 'possible coffee?'. Because there is no subject, 'мо́жна' has nothing to agree with and never changes.

Followed by an infinitive, 'мо́жна' says that an action is allowed or possible, and as a question it asks permission: 'Мо́жна приміря́ти?', literally 'possible to-try-on?', 'May I try it on?'. The sentence names no person. Who would do the action is clear from the situation: in a shop it is the customer, so English says 'May I...?', and in a general question about a place English says 'Can one...?' or 'Can you...?'.

The pattern builds like this:

- An object of the infinitive follows it in the accusative: 'Мо́жна приміря́ти цю су́кню?'
- A word of place or a question word can come first: 'Тут мо́жна сиді́ти?', 'Де мо́жна приміря́ти?'
- 'Чи' can open the question, as with any yes or no question: 'Чи мо́жна приміря́ти?'
- The answer repeats the word: 'Так, мо́жна.' or 'Ні, не мо́жна.'
- 'Не мо́жна', written as two words, says that something is not allowed: 'Тут не мо́жна ї́сти.'

'Мо́жна' is related to the verb 'могти́' ('мо́жу', 'мо́жеш'), but the two are built differently. 'Могти́' is a verb: it has a subject and an ending for each person ('Я мо́жу приміря́ти?', 'Can I try it on?'). 'Мо́жна' names no one and is the usual polite way to ask permission in a shop, a café or an office.

rows: May I try on this dress?
Where can I try it on?

examples.source: Where can you buy bread here?
May I try on these pants?
Yes, you may. Over there, on the left.

culture.title: Markets, sizes and the embroidered shirt
culture.text:
In Ukrainian cities people buy clothes in shopping centers and small shops, but also at open-air markets, where stalls sell clothes and shoes next to food. Secondhand clothing shops are common and cheap. At a market stall the price is sometimes open to a little bargaining; in a shop it is fixed. Prices are in hryvnias. A new jacket in a city shop often costs a few thousand hryvnias, and the numbers above a hundred come in a later unit.

Sizes are numbers, said after the word 'ро́змір':

- women's clothes: 42, 44, 46 and so on
- men's jackets and shirts: 48, 50, 52 and so on
- shoes: from about 36 to 46

Many shops also use the letters S, M and L.

The best-known piece of Ukrainian clothing is 'вишива́нка', an embroidered shirt; the word comes from the verb 'вишива́ти', to embroider. It is worn by men and women, and every region has its own patterns and colors, although red and black thread on white cloth is among the most common. Many people wear one on Vyshyvanka Day, the third Thursday of May, and at weddings and holidays.

Two of the colors in this unit are the colors of the flag of Ukraine, which has a blue stripe above a yellow one. The blue is often said to stand for the sky and the yellow for fields of wheat. Ukrainians often call the flag 'си́ньо-жо́втий', blue-and-yellow. It is a compound adjective: the stem of 'си́ній' with the linking vowel '-о-', written 'ьо' after the soft 'н', is joined by a hyphen to 'жо́втий', and only the second part takes endings.

exercises.prompt: Match each color with its English name
Match each word with its English meaning

choices: [w], as in 'cow', because it comes before a consonant
[ʋ], between English 'v' and 'w', because it comes before a vowel
exercises.explanation: At the end of a syllable, before a consonant, 'в' is [w]: [ˈʒɔwtɪj]. It is [ʋ] only before a vowel, as in 'черво́ний', and it never turns into [f].

choices: As a soft sound, because 'к' follows it
exercises.explanation: Ukrainian 'ч' is hard before every vowel and before a consonant, and it is only slightly softened before 'і'. The soft sign never follows it.

exercises.prompt: Why is the 'я' form of 'купува́ти' spelled 'купу́ю'?
choices: The verb belongs to the second conjugation
The 'в' turns into 'ю' before an ending
In the present, '-ува-' becomes '-у-', as in 'працюва́ти' and 'працю́ю'
exercises.explanation: Verbs in '-ува́ти' replace '-ува-' with '-у-' in the present and take first-conjugation endings: 'купу́ю', 'купу́єш', 'купу́ють'.
'Су́кня' is feminine singular, so 'this' is 'ця'.
'Ку́ртку' is the object, in the accusative, and the feminine form 'ця' becomes 'цю' there, just as 'ку́ртка' becomes 'ку́ртку'.
'Штани́' is a plural-only noun, so the adjective takes the plural ending '-і': 'дорогі́'.
'Гро́ші' has only plural forms, so every word that agrees with it is plural: 'ці гро́ші', even though English says 'this money'.

exercises.hint_source: How much do your new shoes cost?
exercises.explanation: The shoes are the subject, and 'череви́ки' is plural, so the verb is 'ко́штують'. One thing takes 'ко́штує'.

exercises.hint_source: Sam is trying on a jacket.
exercises.explanation: 'Приміря́ти' is conjugated like 'чита́ти', so the form for 'він' is 'приміря́є'.

exercises.prompt_target: Я не хо́чу цю су́кню, я хо́чу ___.
exercises.hint_source: I don't want this dress, I want that one.
exercises.explanation: The noun is left out because it is clear. 'That' for a feminine object in the accusative is 'ту', as 'ця' becomes 'цю'.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'This shirt is white'?
exercises.explanation: 'Ця' agrees with 'соро́чка', and the color after the noun is the predicate. 'Це бі́ла соро́чка.' means 'This is a white shirt', and 'Та соро́чка бі́ла.' means 'That shirt is white'.

exercises.prompt: In 'Це черво́на су́кня.', what does 'це' do?
choices: It is the feminine form of 'цей' and agrees with 'су́кня'
It points at the dress and never changes: 'This is a red dress.'
It asks a question about the dress
exercises.explanation: This 'це' is the pointer: it introduces a whole noun phrase of any gender. The feminine of 'цей' is 'ця', as in 'Ця су́кня черво́на.', 'This dress is red'.

exercises.prompt: In the dress shop, Olena asks 'А ту зеле́ну ти ба́чиш?' What does she mean?
choices: And do you see that green one?
And do you see this green one?
And do you like the green color?
exercises.explanation: 'Ту' is the accusative of 'та', 'that', and the noun 'су́кню' is left out. 'This' would be 'цю'.

exercises.prompt: In 'Мо́жна приміря́ти?', what is the grammatical subject?
choices: 'Я', left out because the ending shows it
There is none: 'мо́жна' is the predicate of a sentence with no subject
exercises.explanation: 'Мо́жна' is a predicative word. It has no person endings and never changes, because the sentence has no subject; the situation shows who would act.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'Ці штани́ сі́рі', with plural words, about one pair of pants?
choices: The sentence is about two pairs of pants
'Штани́' is the plural of a word for one leg of a pair of pants
'Штани́' has no singular, so every word that agrees with it is plural
exercises.explanation: 'Штани́' is a plural-only noun: it names one thing but has only plural forms, so 'ці' and 'сі́рі' are plural too.

exercises.prompt: In the jacket shop, Bohdan says 'Си́ньої нема́є.' Why is 'си́ньої' in the genitive?
choices: 'Нема́є' takes the genitive of what is missing
A color after a verb is always in the genitive
exercises.explanation: 'Нема́є' means 'there is not' and takes the genitive of the thing that is absent. The noun 'ку́ртки' is left out, and 'си́ньої' is the feminine genitive singular of the soft-stem adjective 'си́ній'.

exercises.prompt: Sam tries on a second jacket and says 'Ця не мала́.' Which noun does 'ця' stand for?
exercises.explanation: 'Ця' and 'мала́' are feminine singular, so the noun left out is feminine. 'Ро́змір' is masculine and 'череви́ки' is plural.

exercises.prompt_source: We are buying a yellow dress.
This jacket costs a hundred hryvnias.

exercises.explanation: 'Ця' agrees with the feminine noun 'соро́чка', the color follows as the predicate in the feminine, and there is no word for 'is'.
The jacket is the object, so all three words take the feminine accusative: 'ту чо́рну ку́ртку'.

exercises.prompt_source: How much do these shoes cost?
exercises.explanation: 'Череви́ки' is plural, so 'this' is 'ці' and the verb is 'ко́штують'.

exercises.prompt_source: May I try on this dress?
exercises.explanation: 'Мо́жна' with the infinitive asks permission without naming a person, and the dress, the object of 'приміря́ти', is in the accusative.
